future.name: Future
future.catch: Now it is your turn to learn from history and shape the age.

myth.name: Myth
myth.summary: From the beginning of heaven and earth told in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, to Emperor Jimmu. A story of the country's origins that cannot be measured in years.
myth.catch: The story of this country's beginning, handed down by word of mouth
features: Creation of heaven and earth, and the birth of the land by Izanagi and Izanami
Tales of the gods, including Amaterasu, Susanoo and Okuninushi
After the descent of the heavenly grandson, they lead to Emperor Jimmu's eastern expedition
Myth is not historical fact but a telling of how ancient people saw the world and the country's origins (Kojiki 712, Nihon Shoki 720)
myth.label: Age of the Gods

jomon.name: Jomon
jomon.summary: Hunting, gathering, fishing and settled life. Pottery and pit dwellings, and a rich spiritual culture.
jomon.catch: Ten thousand years of life, beginning with pottery
features: Settled life based on hunting, fishing and gathering spreads
Cord-marked pottery, and ritual objects such as clay figurines
Large settlements such as the Sannai-Maruyama site emerge
They cultivated the wisdom of living with nature's bounty

yayoi.name: Yayoi
yayoi.summary: Rice farming and metalwork spread, and villages grow into small states. Differences in rank appear.
yayoi.catch: Rice farming gave birth to states
features: Rice farming and metalwork arrive from the continent
Surplus creates differences in wealth and status
Moated settlements such as Yoshinogari
Himiko's Yamatai sends envoys to Wei

kofun.name: Kofun
kofun.summary: Keyhole-shaped tombs are built across the land, and the Yamato court unites a wide area.
kofun.catch: Giant tombs tell of the birth of kingship
features: Keyhole-shaped tombs are built in many regions
The Yamato court brings powerful local clans together
Migrants bring technology, Chinese characters and Buddhism
Continental culture is taken in, and the shape of the country forms

asuka.name: Asuka
asuka.summary: Buddhism and continental institutions are adopted, and the foundations of the ritsuryo state are laid.
features: Prince Shotoku sets the Twelve-Level Cap and Rank System and the Seventeen-Article Constitution
Buddhist culture (Asuka culture) blossoms
The Taika Reforms open the road to centralization
Learning from the continent through missions to Sui and Tang

nara.name: Nara
nara.summary: With Heijo-kyo as capital, the ritsuryo system is put in order and Tenpyo culture flowers.
nara.catch: A capital is built, and Buddhism protects the country
features: The capital is placed at Heijo-kyo
The Taiho Code puts the state's machinery in order
The Great Buddha of Todai-ji and the provincial temples
The Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and Man'yoshu are born

heian.name: Heian
heian.summary: From aristocratic government to cloistered rule and the rise of the warriors. Kokufu (Japanese-style) culture is born.
heian.catch: Two faces: elegance and the warrior
features: The move to Heian-kyo, and an era lasting four hundred years
Regency government, and Kokufu culture (The Tale of Genji)
Saicho and Kukai bring new Buddhism
Cloistered rule, and then the rise of the warriors

kamakura.name: Kamakura
kamakura.summary: The warriors take power and run society through the lord–vassal bond of favor and service.
kamakura.catch: The age of the warrior begins
features: Minamoto no Yoritomo opens a shogunate in Kamakura
A lord–vassal relationship of favor and service
The Mongol invasions are repelled, but the shortage of rewards shakes the regime
New Buddhism such as the Pure Land and Zen schools spreads

muromachi.name: Muromachi
muromachi.summary: From the Northern and Southern Courts' conflict to the Onin War and the Warring States. Commoner culture and East Asian trade flourish.
features: The Ashikaga shogunate, and the conflict of the Northern and Southern Courts
Tally trade, and the culture of the Golden and Silver Pavilions
Noh, tea and flower arrangement, culture that continues today
From the Onin War into the Warring States age

azuchi.name: Azuchi–Momoyama
azuchi.summary: Nobunaga and Hideyoshi unify the country. Land surveys and the sword hunt reshape the framework of society.
azuchi.catch: Thirty years of racing toward unification
features: Oda Nobunaga expands his power with firearms and the economy
Toyotomi Hideyoshi carries out land surveys and the sword hunt
Lavish castles such as Azuchi and Osaka
Nanban trade and the arrival of Christianity

edo.name: Edo
edo.summary: About 260 years of the shogunate-domain system. Under peace, cities, townspeople's culture and learning develop.
edo.catch: Two hundred sixty years of peace and townspeople's culture
features: The shogunate-domain system, and a long peace under the closed-country policy
Alternate attendance and the development of the Five Highways
Townspeople's culture such as kabuki, ukiyo-e and haikai
Perry's arrival sets the age in motion

meiji.name: Meiji
meiji.summary: Through the Meiji Restoration, Japan becomes a modern state. Constitution, industry and armed forces are built up rapidly.
meiji.catch: Hurried reforms toward a modern state
features: The Meiji Restoration and civilization and enlightenment
The Constitution of the Empire of Japan and the opening of the Diet
The Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese Wars change Japan's international standing
Modern industry such as railways and factories arises

taisho.name: Taisho
taisho.summary: Taisho Democracy and urban culture. The Great Kanto Earthquake brings a trial.
taisho.catch: The winds of democracy and the modern
features: The Movement to Protect the Constitution, and the appearance of party cabinets
World War I, and boom and bust
The Great Kanto Earthquake (1923)
Mass culture and modern city life

showa.name: Showa
showa.summary: War and defeat, occupation, and then rapid economic growth. More than sixty tumultuous years.
showa.catch: War and recovery, then high growth
features: Depression and the rise of the military, then war
Defeat and occupation, and a new constitution
High-speed growth and the Tokyo Olympics
Through the oil shocks, into the bubble era

heisei.name: Heisei
heisei.summary: Collapse of the bubble and long stagnation, great disasters, informatization and globalization.
heisei.catch: Thirty years of searching after the bubble
features: The bubble bursts, followed by a long economic slump
The Great Hanshin-Awaji and Great East Japan earthquakes
Spread of the internet and mobile phones
Declining birthrate and an aging population advance

reiwa.name: Reiwa
reiwa.summary: Infectious disease, digitalization, AI. History still being made, right now.
features: The spread of COVID-19
Digitalization, and the spread of generative AI
Preparing for disasters, and redesigning society
We ourselves are writing the continuation of history

j001.title: Creation of Heaven and Earth
j001.detail: Heaven and earth separate, and the first gods (such as Ame-no-Minakanushi) appear in the High Plain of Heaven. This is the opening story of the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki.
j001.lesson: Every story begins by telling of a beginning.
j001.label: Age of the Gods

j002.title: Birth of the Islands and the Gods
j002.detail: Izanagi and Izanami stir the sea with a heavenly jeweled spear, give birth to the islands (the Great Eight Islands), and then bear many gods.
j002.lesson: The land was told of as born from the work of the gods.
j002.label: Age of the Gods

j003.title: The Land of the Dead and the Purification
j003.detail: Izanagi follows his dead wife Izanami to the land of the dead, sees what he was forbidden to see, and flees. From his purification, Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo are born.
j003.lesson: Myth reflects ideas of parting, impurity, and cleansing (misogi).
j003.label: Age of the Gods

j004.title: The Heavenly Rock Cave
j004.detail: After Susanoo's violence, Amaterasu hides in a rock cave and the world goes dark. The eight million gods open the cave with cleverness and a dance by Ame-no-Uzume.
j004.lesson: Hard times are overcome through everyone's wisdom and cooperation.
j004.label: Age of the Gods

j005.title: Slaying the Yamata no Orochi
j005.detail: Susanoo, cast out of the High Plain of Heaven, kills the eight-headed serpent in Izumo and saves Princess Kushinada. He finds the sword Kusanagi in its tail.
j005.lesson: Courage and ingenuity can save people from disaster.
j005.label: Age of the Gods

j006.title: Okuninushi Builds the Land
j006.detail: Okuninushi overcomes many trials and, with Sukunabikona, develops the Central Land of Reed Plains (Izumo). He is also known from the tale of the White Hare of Inaba.
j006.lesson: Helping one another and compassion build a country.
j006.label: Age of the Gods

j007.title: The Transfer of the Land
j007.detail: After negotiating with envoys of the heavenly gods, Okuninushi yields the land and is enshrined in a grand palace (Izumo Taisha).
j007.lesson: A tale was left of ruling through talk rather than conflict.
j007.label: Age of the Gods

j008.title: Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
j008.detail: Ninigi, grandson of Amaterasu, receives the Three Sacred Treasures and descends to Takachiho. This is the story of the imperial family's ancestors.
j008.lesson: The sacred treasures are handed down as symbols of authority.
j008.label: Age of the Gods

j009.title: Umisachihiko and Yamasachihiko
j009.detail: The younger brother Yamasachihiko (Hoori) loses his elder brother's fishhook and goes to the sea god's palace. He gains jewels that control the tides and subdues his brother. His grandson becomes Emperor Jimmu.
j009.lesson: Failure can lead to encounters, and even to strength.
j009.label: Age of the Gods

j010.title: Jimmu's Eastern Expedition Begins
j010.detail: The future Emperor Jimmu (Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko) leaves Hyuga and sets out on a long journey east toward Yamato.
j010.lesson: A journey in search of new land became the story of the country's beginning.
j010.label: Age of the Gods

j011.title: Emperor Jimmu Enthroned at Kashihara (Tradition)
j011.detail: The Nihon Shoki says Emperor Jimmu took the throne as the first emperor at Kashihara Palace in Yamato (660 BCE). This became the origin of National Foundation Day. His existence and the date are not confirmed as historical fact.
j011.lesson: Read tradition and fact separately. Even so, how a country told of its own origins is itself history.
j011.label: 660 BCE (traditional)

j012.title: Some of the Oldest Pottery
j012.detail: About 16,000 years ago, pottery begins to be made in the Japanese archipelago, advancing cooking and settled life.
j012.lesson: Technological innovation supports a stable way of life.

j013.title: The Sannai-Maruyama Settlement
j013.detail: A large settlement is built in Aomori, where chestnuts were managed and trade with other regions took place.
j013.lesson: Settled life nurtured networks of exchange and trade.

j014.title: Prayers Embodied in Clay Figurines
j014.detail: Figures expressing prayers for rich harvests and safe childbirth were made in many regions.

j015.title: Rice Farming Spreads
j015.detail: Wet-rice farming and metal tools spread from northern Kyushu to other regions, greatly changing society.
j015.lesson: New technology brought wealth, and also inequality and conflict.

j016.title: The Gold Seal of the King of Na
j016.detail: The Later Han emperor Guangwu is recorded as granting a seal and ribbon to an envoy from the land of Na in Wa.
j016.lesson: Gaining outside authority raised one's standing at home.

j017.title: Himiko Sends an Envoy to Wei
j017.detail: Queen Himiko of Yamatai sends envoys to Wei and is said to have received the title "King of Wa, Friend of Wei."
j017.lesson: International recognition backs up rule at home.

j018.title: Death of Himiko
j018.detail: After Himiko's death the country falls into disorder, and Iyo is said to have been placed on the throne as queen.
j018.lesson: Rule that depends on charisma wavers at the moment of succession.

j019.title: Keyhole-Shaped Tombs Appear
j019.detail: Large keyhole-shaped tombs such as Hashihaka Tomb in Nara are built and spread to many regions.
j019.lesson: A shared tomb form was a visible sign of alliance and order.

j020.title: The Memorial of King Bu of Wa
j020.detail: King Bu of Wa (identified as Emperor Yuryaku) sends envoys to the Song and presents a memorial describing his pacification of the country.
j020.lesson: He sought to raise his country's standing within international relations.

j021.title: Iwai's Rebellion
j021.detail: Iwai, a powerful local lord of Tsukushi, rebels against the Yamato court but is put down.
j021.lesson: The tug-of-war between local autonomy and central control continued.

j022.title: Buddhism Arrives
j022.detail: Buddhist images and scriptures are sent from Baekje (there are theories of 538 and 552).
j022.lesson: Accepting a foreign culture also brings conflict over whether to welcome it.

j023.title: Prince Shotoku as Regent
j023.detail: Under Empress Suiko, Prince Shotoku joins in governing and advances state-building.

j024.title: Twelve-Level Cap and Rank System
j024.detail: A system that promoted people by talent and achievement rather than family background.
j024.lesson: The start of the idea of putting people to use by ability over origin.

j025.title: The Seventeen-Article Constitution
j025.detail: It taught officials proper conduct and stressed the importance of "harmony."
j025.lesson: At its root is a spirit of building consensus to avoid conflict.

j026.title: Missions to Sui China
j026.detail: Ono no Imoko is sent to the Sui to seek equal diplomatic relations and the culture and institutions of the continent.
j026.lesson: An attitude of learning, and the spirit to stand as equals.

j027.title: The Taika Reforms
j027.detail: Prince Naka no Oe and Nakatomi no Kamatari kill Soga no Iruka, and the building of a new state begins.
j027.lesson: Reform begins with a bold decision and trustworthy comrades.

j028.title: Battle of Hakusukinoe
j028.detail: The Wa forces who helped restore Baekje are crushed by Tang and Silla, and the country hurries to build up its defenses.
j028.lesson: An expedition without information and preparation endangers a country.

j029.title: The Jinshin War
j029.detail: After Emperor Tenji's death, Prince Oama defeats Prince Otomo and later becomes Emperor Tenmu.
j029.lesson: A succession struggle can become a crisis that splits a country in two.

j030.title: Capital Moved to Fujiwara-kyo
j030.detail: The first full-scale walled capital, with a grid-pattern city plan introduced.

j031.title: Taiho Code
j031.detail: The ritsuryo codes are completed, setting up a framework of rule by law.
j031.lesson: Put rules in writing and make them the machinery that runs the country.

j032.title: Capital Moved to Heijo-kyo
j032.detail: A capital modeled on Tang Chang'an is built in Nara.
j032.lesson: A city is a mirror reflecting the shape of the state.

j033.title: Kojiki Completed
j033.detail: The oldest surviving history of Japan, recording myths and traditions.

j034.title: Perpetual Private Ownership of Reclaimed Land
j034.detail: Private ownership of newly cultivated land is permitted, the start of the later spread of shoen estates.
j034.lesson: A loophole in the system creates the next order.

j035.title: Eye-Opening of the Great Buddha at Todai-ji
j035.detail: The Great Buddha, vowed by Emperor Shomu, is completed and the eye-opening ceremony is held.
j035.lesson: The fruit of a prayer by the whole nation and the labor of its people.

j036.title: Ganjin Comes to Japan
j036.detail: The Tang high monk Ganjin reaches Japan after great hardship and transmits the monastic precepts.
j036.lesson: Some people carried learning across, at the risk of their lives.

j037.title: Capital Moved to Heian-kyo
j037.detail: Emperor Kanmu moves the capital to Kyoto, which prospers as the capital for a long time after.
j037.lesson: He even moved the capital to renew politics.

j038.title: Saicho and Kukai Go to Tang China
j038.detail: The two travel to Tang on the envoy ships and later found the Tendai and Shingon schools.

j039.title: End of Missions to Tang China
j039.detail: On Sugawara no Michizane's proposal the missions to Tang are halted, and culture turns toward Japanese-style Kokufu culture.
j039.lesson: Reviewing outside ties can let a home culture grow.

j040.title: Taira no Masakado's Rebellion
j040.detail: In the Kanto region, Taira no Masakado calls himself the "New Emperor" and rebels.

j041.title: The Tale of Genji
j041.detail: A long tale by Murasaki Shikibu, which describes in fine detail the human drama of the court.

j042.title: Michinaga Becomes Regent
j042.detail: By marrying his daughters to emperors, the Fujiwara regency reaches its peak.
j042.lesson: A system for concentrating power in one place through marriage.

j043.title: Cloistered Rule Begins
j043.detail: Retired Emperor Shirakawa holds real power as retired sovereign after yielding the throne.
j043.lesson: Real power can move outside the formal system.

j044.title: Hogen Rebellion
j044.detail: Warriors are mobilized in a dispute within the imperial and regent families, and samurai begin to take center stage in politics.

j045.title: Heiji Rebellion
j045.detail: Minamoto no Yoshitomo is defeated and Taira no Kiyomori expands his power.

j046.title: Taira no Kiyomori Becomes Chancellor
j046.detail: He becomes the first warrior to hold the post of Chancellor and builds the Taira government.

j047.title: Honen Preaches Exclusive Nembutsu
j047.detail: Honen founds the Jodo school and teaches salvation through the nembutsu.

j048.title: Minamoto no Yoritomo Raises an Army
j048.detail: After rising against the Taira, he makes Kamakura his base and brings the warriors of eastern Japan under him.
j048.lesson: A cause and a base to unite people's hearts become the core of power.

j049.title: Battle of Dan-no-ura
j049.detail: Minamoto no Yoshitsune and others destroy the Taira, ending the Genpei War.
j049.lesson: Not only victory but the design of rule afterward was put to the test.

j050.title: Shugo and Jito Established
j050.detail: Yoritomo is permitted to appoint shugo and jito, solidifying the foundation of warrior government.
j050.lesson: A system that places people on the ground makes rule effective.

j051.title: Yoritomo Becomes Shogun
j051.detail: Appointed Seii Taishogun by the court, the Kamakura shogunate takes shape (1192 is the conventional date).
j051.lesson: How to combine formal authority with actual power.

j052.title: Buddhist Statues by Unkei and Kaikei
j052.detail: The Kongo Rikishi guardians at the Great South Gate of Todai-ji are made, showing powerful realist sculpture.

j053.title: Jokyu War
j053.detail: Retired Emperor Go-Toba tries to overthrow the shogunate but is defeated, and the shogunate's rule extends to western Japan.

j054.title: Goseibai Shikimoku
j054.detail: Hojo Yasutoki compiles warrior customs into standards for fair judgment.
j054.lesson: Putting unspoken rules in writing creates trust.

j055.title: First Mongol Invasion (Bun'ei)
j055.detail: Yuan and Goryeo forces attack Hakata Bay. The Japanese struggle against massed tactics and firearms.

j056.title: Second Mongol Invasion (Koan)
j056.detail: The Yuan army attacks again but is repelled, helped by defensive walls and a storm.
j056.lesson: Preparing for crisis created later burdens (a shortage of rewards).

j057.title: Einin Debt Relief Order
j057.detail: An order is issued to let vassals recover land they had sold, to relieve their hardship.

j058.title: Fall of the Kamakura Shogunate
j058.detail: Ashikaga Takauji, Nitta Yoshisada and others answer Emperor Go-Daigo's call, and the shogunate falls.
j058.lesson: A regime with piled-up grievances can collapse at a single trigger.

j059.title: Kemmu Restoration
j059.detail: Emperor Go-Daigo aims for emperor-centered rule but provokes warrior discontent.
j059.lesson: Ideals were not enough; the consent of those carrying them out was needed.

j060.title: Northern and Southern Courts Split
j060.detail: The imperial court divides into the Northern Court in Kyoto and the Southern Court in Yoshino, lasting about 60 years.

j061.title: Ashikaga Takauji Becomes Shogun
j061.detail: Appointed Seii Taishogun by the Northern Court, he establishes the Muromachi shogunate.

j062.title: Reunification of the Courts
j062.detail: The Northern and Southern Courts are united under Ashikaga Yoshimitsu.

j063.title: Construction of the Golden Pavilion
j063.detail: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu builds the Kitayama villa. Kitayama culture blends court-noble and warrior culture.

j064.title: Japan–Ming Trade Begins
j064.detail: Official trade using tally licenses begins, importing copper coins and raw silk.
j064.lesson: Trade brings wealth and culture, and funds the regime.

j065.title: Onin War
j065.detail: A succession dispute in the shogun's house and other issues erupt into war, Kyoto burns, and the Warring States age begins.
j065.lesson: A succession dispute spread distrust of the system.

j066.title: Construction of the Silver Pavilion
j066.detail: Ashikaga Yoshimasa builds the Higashiyama villa and nurtures the simple, profound Higashiyama culture.

j067.title: Firearms Arrive
j067.detail: Portuguese are cast ashore on Tanegashima and guns are introduced. The way of fighting changes completely.
j067.lesson: New technology changes the shape of war and the balance of social power.

j068.title: Christianity Arrives
j068.detail: Francis Xavier lands at Kagoshima and begins missionary work.
j068.lesson: The arrival of religion and ideas went hand in hand with trade.

j069.title: Battle of Okehazama
j069.detail: Oda Nobunaga defeats Imagawa Yoshimoto with a small force and makes his name.
j069.lesson: With information and surprise, a numerical disadvantage can be overturned.

j070.title: End of the Muromachi Shogunate
j070.detail: Nobunaga expels Ashikaga Yoshiaki from Kyoto, and the Muromachi shogunate effectively ends.

j071.title: Battle of Nagashino
j071.detail: Nobunaga and Ieyasu use firearms effectively to defeat Takeda Katsuyori's army.
j071.lesson: Combining new technology with organization decided the outcome.

j072.title: Construction of Azuchi Castle
j072.detail: A castle with a magnificent keep rises on the shore of Lake Biwa, becoming a symbol of new authority.

j073.title: Taiko Land Survey
j073.detail: Hideyoshi conducts land surveys across the country and measures the productivity of fields in koku.
j073.lesson: Grasping reality in numbers is the foundation of rule.

j074.title: Honno-ji Incident
j074.detail: Akechi Mitsuhide kills Nobunaga, and Hideyoshi then defeats Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki and takes the lead.
j074.lesson: Even supreme power has a blind spot in discontent at its feet.

j075.title: Sword Hunt Edict
j075.detail: Weapons are collected from farmers, aiming at the separation of warriors and farmers and social stability.

j076.title: Hideyoshi Unifies the Country
j076.detail: He subdues the Hojo of Odawara and brings the long Warring States turmoil to an end.

j077.title: Bunroku Campaign
j077.detail: Hideyoshi sends troops to Korea (1592–93). The Keicho Campaign (1597–98) followed.
j077.lesson: Ambition for expansion cost heavy sacrifices at home and abroad.

j078.title: Battle of Sekigahara
j078.detail: Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern Army defeats Ishida Mitsunari's Western Army and takes supremacy.
j078.lesson: The decisive battle was settled by alliances and an information war.

j079.title: Edo Shogunate Founded
j079.detail: Ieyasu becomes Seii Taishogun and opens the shogunate in Edo.

j080.title: Summer Siege of Osaka
j080.detail: The Toyotomi are destroyed, and a long age of peace begins.

j081.title: Alternate Attendance Institutionalized
j081.detail: The system of daimyo traveling between Edo and their domains is set, promoting the highways and Edo's prosperity.
j081.lesson: Daimyo were controlled through travel and expense.

j082.title: Shimabara Rebellion
j082.detail: People suffering under heavy taxes and the suppression of Christianity rise up.
j082.lesson: When oppression piles up, resistance becomes a great force.

j083.title: Closed-Country Policy Completed
j083.detail: Portuguese ships are banned from coming. Limited exchange continues through Nagasaki and other ports.
j083.lesson: Managed exchange brings stability, but narrows the window of information.

j084.title: Great Fire of Meireki
j084.detail: A great fire burns most of Edo. Fire prevention and the redevelopment of the city advanced afterward.
j084.lesson: Disaster becomes a chance to rethink how a city is built.

j085.title: Journey of "Narrow Road to the Deep North"
j085.detail: Matsuo Basho travels through Tohoku and Hokuriku and raises haikai poetry to an art.

j086.title: Kyoho Reforms
j086.detail: Tokugawa Yoshimune works on fiscal recovery and legal reform, and sets up a suggestion box.
j086.lesson: A system to gather voices from the ground supports reform.

j087.title: Kaitai Shinsho Published
j087.detail: Sugita Genpaku and others translate a Dutch anatomy book, leading to the growth of Dutch learning.
j087.lesson: An attitude of learning other countries' knowledge became the base of modern science.

j088.title: Great Tenmei Famine
j088.detail: Eruptions of Mt. Asama and cold weather bring crop failure, and many people die across the land.

j089.title: Ino Tadataka's Surveys
j089.detail: Beginning his survey in Ezo, he sets in motion a project to measure all of Japan on foot.
j089.lesson: Patient accumulation of real measurements produces accurate maps.

j090.title: Ino's Map Completed
j090.detail: After Tadataka's death, his disciples complete the map of Japan.

j091.title: Thirty-six Views of Mt. Fuji
j091.detail: A series of ukiyo-e prints by Katsushika Hokusai, which later influenced art overseas.

j092.title: Perry Arrives
j092.detail: The Black Ships come to Uraga and demand the opening of the country.
j092.lesson: Outside pressure brings internal contradictions to the surface all at once.

j093.title: Treaty of Kanagawa
j093.detail: Shimoda and Hakodate are opened, and the long-lasting closed-country system turns around.

j094.title: Treaties of Amity and Commerce
j094.detail: Including the US–Japan Treaty of Amity and Commerce. They were unequal, lacking tariff autonomy and granting extraterritoriality.

j095.title: Satsuma–Choshu Alliance
j095.detail: The rival Satsuma and Choshu domains join hands and move toward overthrowing the shogunate.
j095.lesson: Even yesterday's enemies can team up for a shared goal.

j096.title: Restoration of Imperial Rule
j096.detail: Tokugawa Yoshinobu returns political power to the court, and the Edo shogunate ends.

j097.title: Bloodless Surrender of Edo Castle
j097.detail: In a meeting between Saigo Takamori and Katsu Kaishu, the general assault on Edo is avoided.
j097.lesson: Dialogue can save many lives and a whole city.

j098.title: Meiji Restoration
j098.detail: The Charter Oath is issued, and the new government begins building a modern state.
j098.lesson: Changing an old framework requires a shared new goal.

j099.title: Abolition of Domains
j099.detail: Domains are abolished and prefectures established, laying the foundation of a centralized state.

j100.title: Education System Order
j100.detail: Aiming at schooling for all, a policy of placing schools throughout the country is announced.
j100.lesson: Investment in education became the base of modernization.

j101.title: Japan's First Railway
j101.detail: A railway opens between Shimbashi and Yokohama, and the flow of goods and people begins to change.

j102.title: Land Tax Reform
j102.detail: Taxes were changed to be paid in cash according to the value of the land.
j102.lesson: Stable tax revenue supported running the state.

j103.title: Satsuma Rebellion
j103.detail: Saigo Takamori and others take up arms in the last large-scale civil war in Japan.

j104.title: Constitution of the Empire of Japan
j104.detail: Promulgated as a constitution for a constitutional monarchy, with the Diet opened the following year.
j104.lesson: Setting rules for power determines the shape of a country.

j105.title: First Sino-Japanese War
j105.detail: War breaks out from the dispute over Korea. Taiwan and other territory were gained under the Treaty of Shimonoseki.

j106.title: Russo-Japanese War
j106.detail: Japan fights Russia over Manchuria and Korea and makes peace by the Treaty of Portsmouth.
j106.lesson: Behind the victory, the limits of national strength and public discontent also piled up.

j107.title: Annexation of Korea
j107.detail: Japan annexes Korea and carries out colonial rule.
j107.lesson: A history of expansion leaves later friction and responsibility.

j108.title: Entry into World War I
j108.detail: Citing the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, Japan declares war on Germany and extends its influence in Asia.

j109.title: Rice Riots
j109.detail: Protests by people angered by soaring rice prices spread across the country.

j110.title: Founding of the National Levelers' Association
j110.detail: People seeking liberation from discrimination formed their own organization.

j111.title: Great Kanto Earthquake
j111.detail: An earthquake centered off Sagami Bay and the fires that followed devastate the capital region.
j111.lesson: Preparation and accurate information save lives. The tragedy of rumors must not be forgotten either.

j112.title: Universal Manhood Suffrage Law
j112.detail: Men aged 25 and over are given the vote. The Peace Preservation Law was also enacted that year.
j112.lesson: The expansion of rights and the tightening of control advanced together.

j113.title: Great Depression
j113.detail: The world slump spreads to Japan and hits life in farm villages and cities directly.

j114.title: Manchurian Incident
j114.detail: The Kwantung Army blows up a railway at Liutiaohu and widens its occupation of Manchuria.
j114.lesson: Failing to stop the field army's runaway opened the road to war.

j115.title: February 26 Incident
j115.detail: Young Army officers rise up and attack politicians. The military's voice grows stronger.

j116.title: Second Sino-Japanese War Begins
j116.detail: Starting from the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, it widens into full-scale war and drags on.

j117.title: Outbreak of the Pacific War
j117.detail: With attacks such as Pearl Harbor, war begins with the US and Britain.
j117.lesson: A calm view of the gap in national strength and of information is essential.

j118.title: End of the War
j118.detail: After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan accepts the Potsdam Declaration and the war ends.
j118.lesson: Remember the sacrifices of war, and vow never to repeat it.

j119.title: Constitution of Japan Promulgated
j119.detail: A constitution based on popular sovereignty, fundamental human rights and pacifism is promulgated.

j120.title: Peace Treaty Signed
j120.detail: Japan signs the San Francisco Peace Treaty and recovers sovereignty the following year.

j121.title: Tokyo Olympics and the Shinkansen
j121.detail: The Tokyo Olympics are held and the Tokaido Shinkansen opens.
j121.lesson: A goal pursued by the whole nation built infrastructure and confidence.

j122.title: Return of Okinawa
j122.detail: Okinawa returns to Japan, and the same year diplomatic relations with China are normalized.

j123.title: Oil Crisis
j123.detail: Soaring crude oil prices push up prices, and the period of rapid economic growth ends.
j123.lesson: A society that depends on resources is vulnerable to outside change.

j124.title: Era Name Changes to Heisei
j124.detail: Emperor Showa dies and the era name changes to Heisei.

j125.title: Collapse of the Bubble
j125.detail: A sharp fall in stock and land prices ushers in a long economic slump.
j125.lesson: Overheated expectations are eventually pulled back to reality.

j126.title: Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake
j126.detail: A magnitude-7 intensity earthquake damages the city. It is also called the first year of volunteering.
j126.lesson: Urban disasters call for preparation and mutual help.

j127.title: Global Financial Crisis
j127.detail: A financial crisis from the US spreads worldwide, and Japan's economy also falls sharply.

j128.title: Great East Japan Earthquake
j128.detail: A huge earthquake, a tsunami and a nuclear accident combine into an unprecedented disaster.
j128.lesson: Prepare for the unexpected, and pass records and lessons on to the future.

j129.title: Start of Reiwa
j129.detail: With the imperial succession, the era name changes from Heisei to Reiwa.

j130.title: COVID-19 Spreads
j130.detail: The infectious disease spreads worldwide, greatly changing how we work, learn and live.
j130.lesson: The crisis pushed society's digitalization forward all at once.

j131.title: Tokyo Olympics Held
j131.detail: Postponed by a year, they were held without spectators at most venues.

j132.title: Generative AI Spreads
j132.detail: Conversational AI is opened to the public, and the way intellectual work is done begins to change.
j132.lesson: When a new tool appears, that is the time to learn from history.

j133.title: Noto Peninsula Earthquake
j133.detail: A magnitude-7 intensity earthquake strikes Noto, causing severe damage.

j134.title: Osaka-Kansai Expo
j134.detail: An Expo is held in Osaka, where countries around the world showcase the latest technology and culture.

j135.title: Anti-Frame Theory
j135.detail: The note account "ANTI FRAME" publishes the Anti-Frame Theory. It later moved its activities from note to not/on.

j136.title: youside Launched
j136.detail: Matsuyama Daika and Origuchi Jin and others launch "youside.me," a group aiming to implement a digital commons. At the same time, they release "EduMuse," an English vocabulary learning service based on cognitive science.

j137.title: Updated to Theory 2.0
j137.detail: "ANTI FRAME" updates the Anti-Frame Theory to version 2.0.

j138.title: Jomon Transgression
j138.detail: Climate warming raises sea levels and the sea reaches far inland. Shell mounds are clues to the coastline of the time.
j138.lesson: Environmental change changes the very place where people live.

j139.title: Obsidian Trade
j139.detail: Obsidian from Wada Pass, Kozushima and elsewhere is carried to distant settlements, showing the Jomon people's wide exchange network.
j139.lesson: The movement of things is also the movement of people and connections.

j140.title: Flame-Style Pottery
j140.detail: Along the Shinano River basin in Niigata and elsewhere, pots with flame-like decoration are made.
j140.lesson: They poured this much sense of form into everyday goods.

j141.title: Venus of Jomon
j141.detail: From the Tanabatake site in Chino, Nagano, a National Treasure clay figurine of a woman with a full figure has been unearthed.

j142.title: Goggle-Eyed Figurines
j142.detail: Clay figurines with large eyes, typified by the Kamegaoka site in Aomori. They convey the spiritual culture of late Jomon Tohoku.

j143.title: Spread of Paddy Rice Farming
j143.detail: Early paddy fields have been found at sites such as Itazuke and Nabatake in Fukuoka. Rice farming spread east from northern Kyushu.

j144.title: Moated Settlement at Yoshinogari
j144.detail: The Yoshinogari site in Saga is a large Yayoi settlement with deep moats and watchtowers. It shows the progress of conflict and integration.

j145.title: Bronze Bells, Swords and Spears
j145.detail: Bronze objects were used as ritual tools, with different preferred types in each region.

j146.title: The Toro Paddy Fields
j146.detail: At the Toro site in Shizuoka, paddy ridges and wooden farm tools were found, showing what Yayoi rice farming was like.

j147.title: King Suisho of Wa Sends an Envoy to Later Han
j147.detail: The Book of the Later Han records that King Suisho of Wa and others presented 160 seikō (captives or slaves).

j148.title: The Great Wa Disturbance
j148.detail: In the later 2nd century, turmoil continued in Wa. The Wei Zhi (Records of Wa) says it was later settled when the states jointly set up Himiko as queen.

j149.title: Iyo Sends an Envoy to Western Jin
j149.detail: Iyo (Toyo), who succeeded Himiko, is thought to have sent an envoy to the Western Jin.

j150.title: Wa Sends Troops to the Korean Peninsula
j150.detail: The Gwanggaeto Stele of Goguryeo records that Wa crossed the sea and subjugated Baekje and Silla (an entry for 391).

j151.title: King San of Wa Sends an Envoy to Song
j151.detail: The Book of Song records that King San of Wa sent envoys to the Song. It is the first entry on the Five Kings of Wa (San, Chin, Sei, Ko, Bu).

j152.title: Daisen Tomb Built
j152.detail: The Daisen Tomb in Sakai (said to be the tomb of Emperor Nintoku) is Japan's largest keyhole-shaped tomb, about 480 m long. It is thought to date from the mid-5th century.

j153.title: Inscription on the Inariyama Sword
j153.detail: An iron sword from the Inariyama Tomb in Saitama carries a 115-character inscription saying its owner served "Great King Wakatakeru" (a theory dates it to 471).

j154.title: Teibi Disturbance
j154.detail: Soga no Umako, who accepts Buddhism, fights Mononobe no Moriya, who opposes it, and the Mononobe clan is destroyed.

j155.title: Assassination of Emperor Sushun
j155.detail: Emperor Sushun, in conflict with Soga no Umako, is assassinated. Empress Suiko soon takes the throne.

j156.title: Horyu-ji Founded
j156.detail: Horyu-ji, said to have been built at Ikaruga by Prince Shotoku, is one of the world's oldest surviving groups of wooden buildings.

j157.title: Pei Shiqing Visits Japan
j157.detail: Pei Shiqing, an envoy of the Sui, comes to Japan accompanying Ono no Imoko on his return. A reply to the letter that sought equal diplomacy.

j158.title: First Mission to Tang China
j158.detail: Inukami no Mitasuki and others are sent to Tang. From then on, the missions became a channel for bringing back Tang institutions, culture and Buddhism.

j159.title: Edict of Reform
j159.detail: An edict setting out policies such as public ownership of land and people and the allotment of rice fields. It is seen as the starting point of the later ritsuryo state.

j160.title: Fall of Baekje
j160.detail: A Tang–Silla allied army destroys Baekje. Japan tries to help restore Baekje.

j161.title: Enthronement of Emperor Tenji
j161.detail: Prince Naka no Oe takes the throne at Omi Otsu Palace. He is also said to have established the Omi Code.

j162.title: Koin Nenjaku Register
j162.detail: Regarded as Japan's first nationwide household register. It became the basis for later land allotment and conscription.

j163.title: Asukakiyomihara Code
j163.detail: The code compiled from the time of Emperor Tenmu was put into force under Empress Jito. An intermediate step in building the ritsuryo state.

j164.title: Resumption of Missions to Tang China
j164.detail: Awata no Mahito and others cross to Tang. At this time, the national name "Nihon" is said to have been used.

j165.title: Minting of Wado Kaichin
j165.detail: After copper is presented from Musashi Province, Wado Kaichin coins are issued. One of Japan's early circulating currencies.

j166.title: Order to Compile the Fudoki
j166.detail: Provinces are ordered to report the origins of place names, local products and traditions. Works such as the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki survive.

j167.title: Nihon Shoki Completed
j167.detail: An official history in classical Chinese compiled by Prince Toneri and others. It covers the period from the age of the gods to Empress Jito.

j168.title: Sanze Isshin Law
j168.detail: A law allowing newly cultivated land to be privately held for three generations (or one).

j169.title: Incident of Prince Nagaya
j169.detail: Prince Nagaya, Minister of the Left, is driven to suicide on suspicion of treason, and the Fujiwara expand their power.

j170.title: Great Smallpox Epidemic
j170.detail: A plague spreading from Kyushu kills the four Fujiwara brothers one after another (737). It caused a large drop in population.

j171.title: Rebellion of Fujiwara no Hirotsugu
j171.detail: A revolt in Kyushu. Shaken, Emperor Shomu kept moving the capital from place to place.

j172.title: Edict to Build Provincial Temples
j172.detail: To calm plague and war through the power of the Buddha, provinces were ordered to build kokubun-ji and kokubun-niji temples.

j173.title: Toshodai-ji Founded
j173.detail: A temple built by Ganjin. Its Golden Hall conveys the look of the Nara period to the present.

j174.title: The Last Poem in the Man'yoshu
j174.detail: A poem by Otomo no Yakamochi (759) placed last in the Man'yoshu, Japan's oldest poetry anthology with about 4,500 poems.

j175.title: Hyakumanto Darani
j175.detail: Empress Shotoku had sutras placed inside a million small pagodas. They are regarded as among the oldest surviving printed materials.

j176.title: Capital Moved to Nagaoka-kyo
j176.detail: To get away from the Buddhist powers of Nara, Emperor Kanmu moves the capital to Nagaoka in Yamashiro. Ten years later it moved to Heian-kyo.

j177.title: Hieizan-ji Founded
j177.detail: Saicho opens Ichijo Shikan-in on Mt. Hiei. It later became Enryaku-ji.

j178.title: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro Becomes Shogun
j178.detail: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro is appointed Seii Taishogun to campaign against the Emishi. He builds Isawa Castle in 802.

j179.title: Mt. Koya Founded
j179.detail: Kukai receives Mt. Koya from Emperor Saga and opens a place of Shingon esoteric practice.

j180.title: Fujiwara no Yoshifusa Becomes Regent
j180.detail: Under the young Emperor Seiwa, Fujiwara no Yoshifusa acts as regent in practice. The first from outside the imperial family.

j181.title: Otenmon Incident
j181.detail: The Otenmon gate of the court is burned, and Ban no Yoshio and others are punished. One of the Fujiwara's expulsions of rival clans.

j182.title: Fujiwara no Mototsune Becomes Kampaku
j182.detail: With the accession of Emperor Koko, Fujiwara no Mototsune takes charge of government. This set the precedent for the kampaku.

j183.title: Demotion of Sugawara no Michizane
j183.detail: Michizane, Minister of the Right, is demoted to Dazaifu. He later came to be worshipped as "Tenjin-sama."

j184.title: Kokin Wakashu
j184.detail: The first imperially commissioned poetry anthology, compiled by Ki no Tsurayuki and others at Emperor Daigo's order. Its kana preface speaks of the heart of poetry.

j185.title: Tosa Diary
j185.detail: Written by Ki no Tsurayuki in the guise of a woman, the beginning of diary literature in kana.

j186.title: Death of Taira no Masakado
j186.detail: Masakado, who styled himself "New Emperor" in Hitachi and Shimosa, is killed by Fujiwara no Hidesato and others.

j187.title: Rebellion of Fujiwara no Sumitomo
j187.detail: A revolt by Sumitomo, who led pirates of the Seto Inland Sea. Together with Masakado's rebellion it is called the Johei-Tengyo Disturbance.

j188.title: Anna Incident
j188.detail: Minamoto no Takaaki is demoted, and the Fujiwara regency government is established.

j189.title: Toi Invasion
j189.detail: A group thought to be Jurchen raids Tsushima, Iki and northern Kyushu. Fujiwara no Takaie and others at Dazaifu repel them.

j190.title: Former Nine Years' War
j190.detail: A war between the Abe clan of Mutsu and the court. Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, helped by the Kiyohara of Dewa, pacify it (1062).

j191.title: Byodo-in Phoenix Hall
j191.detail: An Amida hall built at Uji by Fujiwara no Yorimichi. It represents the Pure Land on earth.

j192.title: Later Three Years' War
j192.detail: Minamoto no Yoshiie intervenes in a dispute within the Kiyohara of Oshu. The victor Fujiwara (Kiyohara) no Kiyohira becomes founder of the Oshu Fujiwara.

j193.title: Konjikido of Chuson-ji
j193.detail: Kiyohira of the Oshu Fujiwara builds an Amida hall covered entirely in gold leaf at Hiraizumi.

j194.title: Capital Moved to Fukuhara
j194.detail: Taira no Kiyomori moves the capital to Fukuhara (Kobe), the hub of Japan–Song trade. It returned to Kyoto in about half a year.

j195.title: Yowa Famine
j195.detail: A great famine centered on western Japan. The sight of the dead filling Kyoto was later described in the Hojoki.

j196.title: Battle of Kurikara Pass
j196.detail: Kiso Yoshinaka defeats a large Taira army and enters Kyoto.

j197.title: Battle of Ichinotani
j197.detail: Minamoto no Yoshitsune and others defeat the Taira with a surprise attack down a cliff (the tradition of the Hiyodorigoe descent).

j198.title: Battle of Yashima
j198.detail: Minamoto no Yoshitsune crosses in a storm and attacks the Taira at Yashima in Sanuki. Known for Nasu no Yoichi's shot at the fan.

j199.title: Fall of the Oshu Fujiwara
j199.detail: Yoritomo sends troops to Oshu and destroys Fujiwara no Yasuhira at Hiraizumi.

j200.title: Death of Minamoto no Yoritomo
j200.detail: After Yoritomo's death, the council of thirteen supporting the young Yoriie and the rise of the Hojo clan begin.

j201.title: Hiki Yoshikazu Incident
j201.detail: Hojo Tokimasa destroys the Hiki clan and confines Shogun Yoriie in Izu.

j202.title: Shin Kokin Wakashu
j202.detail: An imperially commissioned anthology compiled by Fujiwara no Teika and others at the order of Retired Emperor Go-Toba.

j203.title: Hojoki
j203.detail: An essay by Kamo no Chomei, who watched the capital's great fires, earthquakes, famine and relocation, setting down impermanence.

j204.title: Assassination of Minamoto no Sanetomo
j204.detail: The third shogun Sanetomo is assassinated at Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gu in Kamakura, ending the Minamoto line of shoguns.

j205.title: Dogen Returns from Song China
j205.detail: Dogen, who brought the Soto school, returns from Southern Song. He teaches seated meditation, "just sitting" (shikantaza).

j206.title: Nichiren Founds the Hokke School
j206.detail: At Seicho-ji in Awa, Nichiren chants the title "Namu Myoho Renge Kyo" and begins to preach his teaching.

j207.title: Shochu Incident
j207.detail: Emperor Go-Daigo's plan to overthrow the shogunate is discovered.

j208.title: Genko War
j208.detail: Emperor Go-Daigo raises troops against the shogunate. He is defeated at Mt. Kasagi and exiled to Oki, but support spreads in many regions.

j209.title: Kanno Disturbance
j209.detail: The conflict between Ashikaga Takauji and his brother Tadayoshi, a civil war that spread across the country.

j210.title: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu Becomes Shogun
j210.detail: The young Yoshimitsu becomes the third shogun. He later unites the Northern and Southern Courts and stabilizes the shogunate.

j211.title: The Flower Palace
j211.detail: The residence Ashikaga Yoshimitsu built at Muromachi in Kyoto. It gave the "Muromachi shogunate" its name.

j212.title: Fushikaden
j212.detail: A book by Zeami on the art and principles of Noh, known for the phrase "the hidden is the flower."

j213.title: Shocho Peasant Uprising
j213.detail: Carters of Omi rise up demanding debt relief. Regarded as the beginning of popular uprisings.

j214.title: Kakitsu Incident
j214.detail: Akamatsu Mitsusuke assassinates Shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori. The decline of the shogunate's authority advances.

j215.title: Yamashiro Province Uprising
j215.detail: Local lords and farmers of southern Yamashiro drive out the Hatakeyama army and govern themselves for eight years.

j216.title: Kaga Ikko Uprising
j216.detail: Followers of the Ikko sect overthrow the shugo Togashi Masachika, and for about 100 years it was called "the province held by the peasants."

j217.title: Hojo Soun Takes Odawara Castle
j217.detail: Soun, who had taken Izu, gains Odawara Castle and becomes a forerunner of the Sengoku daimyo.

j218.title: Ningbo Incident
j218.detail: Envoys of the Ouchi and Hosokawa clans fight at Ningbo in Ming China. From then on the Ouchi handled the tally trade.

j219.title: Battles of Kawanakajima
j219.detail: Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin face each other repeatedly at Kawanakajima in Shinano. The fiercest battle was in 1561.

j220.title: Battle of Itsukushima
j220.detail: Mori Motonari defeats Sue Harukata with a surprise attack. It was the start of his rise to dominance in the Chugoku region.

j221.title: Oda Nobunaga Enters Kyoto
j221.detail: Backing Ashikaga Yoshiaki, he enters Kyoto and installs Yoshiaki as the 15th shogun.

j222.title: Battle of Anegawa
j222.detail: The Oda–Tokugawa army defeats the Asai–Asakura army at the Ane River in Omi.

j223.title: Burning of Mt. Hiei
j223.detail: Nobunaga burns Enryaku-ji, which had aided his enemies the Asai and Asakura.

j224.title: Rakuichi-Rakuza
j224.detail: Nobunaga abolishes the privileges of guilds (za) and permits free trade in the castle town of Azuchi.

j225.title: Tensho Embassy to Europe
j225.detail: Boy envoys leave for Rome as representatives of the three daimyo Otomo, Omura and Arima.

j226.title: Battle of Shizugatake
j226.detail: Hashiba Hideyoshi defeats Shibata Katsuie and wins the struggle over Nobunaga's succession.

j227.title: Osaka Castle Built
j227.detail: Hideyoshi begins building Osaka Castle on the site of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji.

j228.title: Edict Expelling Missionaries
j228.detail: Hideyoshi orders missionaries to leave the country, though he let trade continue.

j229.title: Kitano Grand Tea Gathering
j229.detail: Hideyoshi holds a great tea gathering at Kitano Tenman-gu in Kyoto, open to people of any status.

j230.title: Seppuku of Sen no Rikyu
j230.detail: By Hideyoshi's order, the tea master Rikyu is made to commit seppuku. There are various theories on the reason.

j231.title: Keicho Campaign
j231.detail: Hideyoshi sends troops to Korea again. The troops withdrew with Hideyoshi's death the following year.

j232.title: Martyrdom of the Twenty-Six Saints of Japan
j232.detail: Twenty-six Christians are executed in Nagasaki.

j233.title: Death of Toyotomi Hideyoshi
j233.detail: The Five Elders and Five Commissioners were to support the young Hideyori, but the conflict between Ieyasu and Mitsunari deepens.

j234.title: Arrival of the Liefde
j234.detail: The Dutch ship Liefde drifts ashore in Bungo. William Adams (Miura Anjin) went into Ieyasu's service.

j235.title: Izumo no Okuni and Kabuki
j235.detail: Izumo no Okuni performs the "kabuki dance" in Kyoto and becomes popular. The beginning of kabuki.

j236.title: Satsuma's Invasion of the Ryukyus
j236.detail: The Shimazu send troops to the Ryukyu Kingdom and make it submit. The Ryukyus kept up ties with Ming and Qing too.

j237.title: Winter Siege of Osaka
j237.detail: The Tokugawa army surrounds Osaka Castle. Known for Sanada Maru, built by Sanada Nobushige (Yukimura).

j238.title: Laws for the Military Houses and One-Castle-per-Province Order
j238.detail: Laws regulating daimyo castles, marriages and conduct. Tokugawa's system of control was solidified.

j239.title: Dutch Trading Post Moved to Dejima
j239.detail: The Dutch trading post at Hirado is moved to Dejima in Nagasaki, and trade is limited to Dutch and Chinese ships.

j240.title: Keian Incident
j240.detail: A plot by Yui Shosetsu and others to overthrow the shogunate is discovered. A growing number of masterless samurai lay behind it.

j241.title: Echigoya Founded
j241.detail: Mitsui Takatoshi opens the drapery store "Echigoya" in Edo and wins popularity with fixed-price cash sales.

j242.title: The Life of an Amorous Man
j242.detail: Ihara Saikaku publishes an ukiyo-zoshi novel depicting how townspeople live, and it becomes a hit.

j243.title: Laws of Compassion for Living Things
j243.detail: The fifth shogun Tsunayoshi bans the killing of living creatures such as dogs.

j244.title: Ako Incident
j244.detail: Asano Naganori draws a sword in Edo Castle and is made to commit seppuku; the next year Oishi Kuranosuke and others carry out the night raid.

j245.title: Genroku Earthquake
j245.detail: A great earthquake strikes southern Kanto. A tsunami hit the coasts of Boso and Sagami.

j246.title: The Love Suicides at Sonezaki
j246.detail: A domestic puppet play by Chikamatsu Monzaemon. Drawn from a real double suicide, it became a great hit.

j247.title: Hoei Earthquake and Eruption of Mt. Fuji
j247.detail: Forty-nine days after a great Nankai Trough earthquake, Mt. Fuji erupts and ash falls on Edo as well.

j248.title: Suggestion Box Established
j248.detail: Yoshimune had commoners submit opinions in writing. It led to things such as the founding of the Koishikawa Infirmary.

j249.title: Great Kyoho Famine
j249.detail: A plague of planthoppers and other causes bring a severe crop failure in western Japan.

j250.title: Kujikata Osadamegaki
j250.detail: The shogunate's legal code compiling standards for trials and punishments.

j251.title: Kanadehon Chushingura
j251.detail: A masterpiece of puppet theater and kabuki, based on the Ako Incident, is first staged.

j252.title: Birth of Nishiki-e
j252.detail: Suzuki Harunobu and others perfect the multicolor ukiyo-e print (nishiki-e).

j253.title: Tanuma Okitsugu Becomes Senior Councillor
j253.detail: He pursued economic policies that valued merchant guilds and trade. There is also criticism that bribery was rampant.

j254.title: Kansei Reforms
j254.detail: Senior Councillor Matsudaira Sadanobu practiced frugality, rice storage and returning farmers to their villages, aiming to restore shogunate finances.

j255.title: Laxman Arrives
j255.detail: A Russian envoy arrives at Nemuro and requests trade.

j256.title: Kojiki-den Completed
j256.detail: Motoori Norinaga's commentary reading the Kojiki, which took 35 years. It brought National Learning to full flower.

j257.title: Phaeton Incident
j257.detail: A British warship enters Nagasaki harbor and takes Dutch trading post staff hostage.

j258.title: Hokusai Manga
j258.detail: Katsushika Hokusai publishes collections of sketches of people, plants, animals and landscapes.

j259.title: Edict to Repel Foreign Ships
j259.detail: The shogunate orders foreign ships approaching the coast to be fired upon and driven away.

j260.title: Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido
j260.detail: Utagawa Hiroshige paints the scenery of the Tokaido, answering the commoners' travel boom.

j261.title: Tenpo Famine
j261.detail: Poor harvests from cold weather and long rains continue for several years. Uprisings and smashings occur in many places.

j262.title: Oshio Heihachiro's Rebellion
j262.detail: Oshio Heihachiro, a former official of the Osaka city magistrate, rises up to save people suffering from the famine.

j263.title: Tenpo Reforms
j263.detail: Senior Councillor Mizuno Tadakuni issues frugality edicts and dissolves merchant guilds, trying to break through the shogunate's fiscal troubles.

j264.title: Firewood and Water Supply Order
j264.detail: Learning of Qing China's defeat in the Opium War, the shogunate revises the Edict to Repel Foreign Ships.

j265.title: Ansei Edo Earthquake
j265.detail: A direct-hit earthquake strikes Edo. Deaths are said to be from several thousand to 10,000.

j266.title: Ansei Purge
j266.detail: Chief Minister Ii Naosuke punishes opposing court nobles, daimyo and loyalist activists.

j267.title: Sakuradamon Incident
j267.detail: Ex-Mito retainers and others assassinate Ii Naosuke outside the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle.

j268.title: Kanrin Maru Crosses the Pacific
j268.detail: Carrying Katsu Kaishu, Fukuzawa Yukichi and others, a Japanese ship crosses the Pacific for the first time.

j269.title: Namamugi Incident
j269.detail: An Englishman who crossed a Satsuma procession is killed and wounded. It led to the Anglo-Satsuma War the next year.

j270.title: Anglo-Satsuma War
j270.detail: In retaliation for the Namamugi Incident, a British fleet bombards Kagoshima. Satsuma then drew closer to Britain.

j271.title: Kinmon Incident
j271.detail: The Choshu domain fights Aizu and Satsuma troops at the Hamaguri Gate of the Kyoto Imperial Palace and is defeated.

j272.title: Ikedaya Incident
j272.detail: At the Ikedaya inn on Sanjo in Kyoto, the Shinsengumi attack Choshu-affiliated loyalists.

j273.title: Paris International Exposition
j273.detail: The shogunate and the Satsuma and Saga domains exhibit. Japanese crafts spurred the European craze for Japonisme.

j274.title: Return of the Domain Registers
j274.detail: Daimyo return their land (han) and people (seki) to the emperor.

j275.title: Battle of Goryokaku
j275.detail: Enomoto Takeaki and other former shogunate forces hold out in Goryokaku in Hakodate and are defeated. The end of the Boshin War.

j276.title: Iwakura Mission
j276.detail: Led by Iwakura Tomomi, it tours Europe and America for about two years. It failed to revise the unequal treaties but gained a guide for modernization.

j277.title: Conscription Ordinance
j277.detail: Imposed the duty of military service on men aged 20. Based on the idea of universal conscription.

j278.title: Political Crisis of 1873
j278.detail: Saigo Takamori, Itagaki Taisuke and others, who lost the debate over invading Korea, leave the government.

j279.title: Petition for a Popularly Elected Assembly
j279.detail: Itagaki Taisuke and others submit to the government a petition demanding the opening of a national assembly. The start of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement.

j280.title: Tokyo University Founded
j280.detail: The government-run University of Tokyo opens. It became the center of higher education in modern Japan.

j281.title: Imperial Rescript on the Opening of the Diet
j281.detail: It promised to open the Diet ten years later (1890).

j282.title: Cabinet System Created
j282.detail: Ito Hirobumi becomes the first prime minister.

j284.title: Imperial Rescript on Education
j284.detail: A document setting out the basis of national education. It was used in school ceremonies and elsewhere.

j285.title: Treaty of Shimonoseki
j285.detail: The peace treaty of the First Sino-Japanese War. Qing ceded Taiwan, the Liaodong Peninsula and more to Japan and paid an indemnity.

j286.title: Triple Intervention
j286.detail: Russia, Germany and France advise Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula.

j287.title: Gold Standard Established
j287.detail: Using the Sino-Japanese War indemnity as reserves, Japan also adopts the gold standard.

j288.title: Yawata Steel Works Starts Operation
j288.detail: The state-run Yawata Steel Works begins operation. It became the base of heavy industry.

j289.title: Anglo-Japanese Alliance
j289.detail: To counter Russia, Japan forms a military alliance with Britain.

j290.title: Treaty of Portsmouth
j290.detail: The peace treaty of the Russo-Japanese War. No indemnity was obtained, and discontent grew at home.

j291.title: Hibiya Incendiary Incident
j291.detail: Discontent with the peace treaty sparks a large riot in Tokyo.

j292.title: Assassination of Ito Hirobumi
j292.detail: He is assassinated at Harbin Station by An Jung-geun, a Korean independence activist.

j293.title: Tariff Autonomy Restored
j293.detail: Under Foreign Minister Komura Jutaro, treaty revision is completed.

j294.title: Death of Emperor Meiji and Start of Taisho
j294.detail: General Nogi Maresuke and his wife follow him in death.

j295.title: Tokyo Station Opens
j295.detail: A red-brick station building designed by Tatsuno Kingo opens in Tokyo.

j296.title: Twenty-One Demands
j296.detail: Japan demands rights in Shandong and elsewhere from China. Anti-Japanese feeling grew in China.

j297.title: Joins the League of Nations
j297.detail: Japan becomes a permanent member of the Council.

j298.title: Washington Conference
j298.detail: Naval arms limits and other matters are discussed, and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance ends (1921–22).

j299.title: Radio Broadcasting Begins
j299.detail: Radio broadcasting starts in Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya, spreading mass culture.

j300.title: Financial Panic
j300.detail: Runs on banks follow one after another, and many banks suspend business.

j301.title: Subway Opens
j301.detail: Japan's first subway opens between Asakusa and Ueno in Tokyo.

j302.title: Assassination of Zhang Zuolin
j302.detail: The Kwantung Army blows up the train of Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin and kills him.

j303.title: May 15 Incident
j303.detail: Young naval officers assassinate Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi. The era of party cabinets ends.

j304.title: Founding of Manchukuo
j304.detail: The Kwantung Army occupies Manchuria and creates Manchukuo.

j305.title: Withdrawal from the League of Nations
j305.detail: Rejecting the recommendation on Manchukuo, Japan leaves the League.

j306.title: Tripartite Pact
j306.detail: Japan forms a military alliance with Germany and Italy. Conflict with the United States deepens.

j307.title: Battle of Midway
j307.detail: The Japanese Navy suffers a crushing defeat, losing four aircraft carriers. A turning point of the war.

j308.title: Fall of Saipan
j308.detail: Japan's defensive line collapses, and air raids on the mainland begin in earnest.

j309.title: Great Tokyo Air Raid
j309.detail: On March 10, Tokyo's downtown is heavily bombed and about 100,000 people die.

j310.title: Battle of Okinawa
j310.detail: US forces land on the main island of Okinawa. A ground battle that engulfed civilians, with many casualties.

j311.title: Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
j311.detail: Atomic bombs are dropped on Hiroshima on August 6 and on Nagasaki on the 9th.

j312.title: Tokyo Trial Opens
j312.detail: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East opens.

j313.title: Constitution of Japan Takes Effect
j313.detail: On May 3, the new constitution comes into force. Now observed as Constitution Memorial Day.

j314.title: Korean War and the National Police Reserve
j314.detail: The Korean War breaks out and the National Police Reserve is created in Japan. The economy recovers through "special procurements."

j315.title: Sovereignty Restored
j315.detail: The San Francisco Peace Treaty takes effect and Japan regains independence.

j316.title: Lucky Dragon No. 5 Incident
j316.detail: Crew of a fishing boat are exposed to radiation from an H-bomb test at Bikini Atoll. The movement to ban atomic and hydrogen bombs spreads.

j317.title: Self-Defense Forces Established
j317.detail: The Defense Agency and the Self-Defense Forces are established.

j318.title: 1955 System
j318.detail: The Liberal Democratic Party is formed, and a two-party structure of conservatives and progressives lasted for a long time.

j319.title: Japan–Soviet Joint Declaration and UN Membership
j319.detail: Relations with the Soviet Union are restored and Japan joins the United Nations.

j320.title: Arson at Kinkaku-ji
j320.detail: An apprentice monk's arson burns down the Golden Pavilion. Mishima Yukio later made it into the novel "The Temple of the Golden Pavilion."

j321.title: Television Broadcasting Begins
j321.detail: NHK starts regular television broadcasting in Tokyo.

j322.title: Tokyo Tower Completed
j322.detail: Built as a broadcasting tower. Height 333 m.

j323.title: Crown Prince's Wedding
j323.detail: People rush to watch the wedding parade broadcast, and television spreads all at once.

j324.title: Anpo Protests
j324.detail: Large-scale demonstrations continue against the revision of the US–Japan Security Treaty.

j325.title: Kawabata Yasunari Wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
j325.detail: The first Japanese to receive the literature prize.

j326.title: Osaka World Exposition
j326.detail: Held on the theme "Progress and Harmony for Mankind," it drew about 64 million visitors.

j327.title: Japan–China Peace and Friendship Treaty
j327.detail: Six years after normalization (1972), the treaty of friendship is concluded.

j328.title: Narita Airport Opens
j328.detail: Amid ongoing opposition to its construction, the New Tokyo International Airport opens.

j329.title: Walkman Released
j329.detail: Sony releases the portable cassette player "Walkman."

j330.title: Family Computer Released
j330.detail: Nintendo's home game console made games a pastime at home.

j331.title: Plaza Accord
j331.detail: An agreement on coordinated intervention to push up the yen and weaken the dollar, later a remote cause of the bubble economy.

j332.title: Crash of Japan Airlines Flight 123
j332.detail: The plane crashes into Osutaka Ridge in Gunma. 520 people died.

j333.title: Breakup and Privatization of Japanese National Railways

j334.title: Non-LDP Coalition Government
j334.detail: The Hosokawa Morihiro cabinet is formed, and the 1955 system ends.

j335.title: Oe Kenzaburo Wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
j335.detail: The second Japanese winner, after Kawabata Yasunari.

j336.title: Tokyo Subway Sarin Attack
j336.detail: Aum Shinrikyo releases sarin on the Tokyo subway.

j337.title: Consumption Tax Raised to 5%
j337.detail: The consumption tax rate is raised from 3% to 5%.

j338.title: Kyoto Protocol
j338.detail: At a conference held in Kyoto, targets for cutting greenhouse gases are adopted.

j339.title: Koizumi Cabinet Formed
j339.detail: A cabinet that championed "structural reform" lasted about five and a half years.

j340.title: Japan–North Korea Summit
j340.detail: Prime Minister Koizumi visits Pyongyang and meets General Secretary Kim Jong Il.

j341.title: Japan–Korea World Cup
j341.detail: The soccer World Cup is co-hosted by Japan and South Korea.

j342.title: Change of Government
j342.detail: The Democratic Party wins a landslide in the House of Representatives election and the Hatoyama cabinet is formed.

j345.title: Kumamoto Earthquakes
j345.detail: Two intensity-7 earthquakes strike in a row in April.

j346.title: Western Japan Floods
j346.detail: Record heavy rain falls over a wide area, killing more than 200 people.

j347.title: Birth of the Three Noble Children
j347.detail: From the purification of Izanagi after returning from the land of the dead, Amaterasu (sun), Tsukuyomi (moon) and Susanoo (sea and storms) are said to be born.

j348.title: Susanoo Banished from the High Plain of Heaven
j348.detail: After repeated violence, Susanoo is punished by the council of the gods, expelled from the High Plain of Heaven and said to have descended to Izumo.
j348.lesson: Force alone does not earn a place in the community.

j349.title: The White Hare of Inaba
j349.detail: The story of Onamuji (later Okuninushi) helping a skinned white hare. It appears in the Kojiki.
j349.lesson: How you treat the weak shapes your stature.

j350.title: Building the Land with Sukunabikona
j350.detail: The small god Sukunabikona and Okuninushi join forces and are said to have spread the arts of farming, medicine and charms.

j351.title: Legend of Izumo Taisha's Founding
j351.detail: The tradition that a grand palace was built for Okuninushi in return for the transfer of the land is said to be the origin of Izumo Taisha.

j352.title: The Three Sacred Treasures
j352.detail: At the descent of the heavenly grandson, a mirror, sword and jewel were bestowed. They are said to be handed down as symbols of the imperial throne.

j353.title: Ninigi and Konohanasakuya-hime
j353.detail: The heavenly grandson Ninigi marries Konohanasakuya-hime, daughter of a mountain god, which leads to the lineage of later gods.

j354.title: The Guide Yatagarasu
j354.detail: When Jimmu's army loses its way in the steep mountains of Kumano, a three-legged crow is said by the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki to have guided them.

j355.title: Battle with Nagasunehiko
j355.detail: As Jimmu's army tries to enter Yamato, the Kiki chronicles say it fought the local chieftain Nagasunehiko.

j356.title: End of the Ice Age
j356.detail: The last ice age ends and warming advances, greatly changing the flora and fauna of the Japanese archipelago.
j356.lesson: Life gets remade to suit changes in the environment.

j357.title: Pit Dwellings Appear
j357.detail: Dwellings dug into the ground and roofed are built in many regions, and settled life spreads.

j358.title: Spread of the Bow and Arrow
j358.detail: To hunt small, fast animals, bows and arrows came into wide use. Stone arrowheads are found in many places.

j359.title: Formation of the Japanese Archipelago
j359.detail: Rising sea levels cut the land connection to the continent, and islands of nearly their present shape take form.

j360.title: Lacquer Ornaments
j360.detail: At sites such as Kakinoshima in Hokkaido, red lacquered ornaments and grave goods have been found. Among the world's oldest lacquer cultures.

j361.title: Giant Eruption of the Kikai Caldera
j361.detail: A huge eruption off southern Kyushu strikes Jomon settlements of southern Kyushu hard with pyroclastic flows and volcanic ash.

j362.title: Use of Dugout Canoes
j362.detail: Dugout canoes have been unearthed from sites such as the Torihama shell mound in Fukui. Fishing and exchange using the sea and lakes thrived.

j363.title: Chestnut Management and Cultivation
j363.detail: At the Sannai-Maruyama site, traces have been found of chestnut trees being managed for food and building material.

j364.title: Jade Trade
j364.detail: Jade from Itoigawa, Niigata was carried north to Hokkaido and south to Okinawa. Beads were Jomon prestige goods.

j365.title: Shell Mounds as "Dumps"
j365.detail: Shell mounds, piled with shells, bones and broken tools, were not only records of diet but also places to mourn the dead.

j366.title: Stone Circles
j366.detail: Ritual sites with stones laid in circles, such as the Oyu Stone Circles in Akita, were made.

j367.title: Stone Rods and Ritual Tools
j367.detail: Ritual tools such as stone rods shaped like men and stone ornaments were made in settlements in many regions.

j368.title: Cooling and Population Decline
j368.detail: After the mid-Jomon period the climate cooled, and settlements shrank, mainly in eastern Japan.

j369.title: Spread of Kamegaoka Culture
j369.detail: Kamegaoka-style pottery of Tohoku, known for its fine coloring and patterns, was carried far and wide.

j370.title: From Jomon to Yayoi
j370.detail: People bringing rice farming and metalwork came from the Korean Peninsula, and life in the archipelago changed over several centuries.

j371.title: Bronze and Iron Arrive
j371.detail: Along with rice farming, bronze and iron came in from the continent. Bronze was used for ritual tools, iron for farm tools and weapons.

j372.title: Raised-Floor Storehouses
j372.detail: Storehouses on tall posts were built to protect rice from rats and damp. Stored wealth produced differences in power.

j373.title: Spread of Moated Settlements
j373.detail: Settlements ringed with moats were prepared for conflict. The Karako-Kagi site in Nara is representative.

j374.title: Jar Burials
j374.detail: In northern Kyushu, the custom of burying the dead in large jars spread. Differences in grave goods suggest differences in rank.

j375.title: Han Establishes Lelang Commandery
j375.detail: Han sets up the Lelang Commandery on the Korean Peninsula. The people of Wa later came to deal with the continent through it.

j376.title: Bronze Swords of Kojindani
j376.detail: At the Kojindani site in Shimane, as many as 358 bronze swords were found in a single place. Bronze bells were later found nearby.

j377.title: Square-Ditched Burial Mounds
j377.detail: Graves marked off by a square ditch spread across regions, and the custom of burying group leaders specially arose.

j378.title: The People of Wa in the Book of Han
j378.detail: It records: "In the sea beyond Lelang there are the people of Wa, divided into more than a hundred states." The Japanese archipelago first appears in written records.

j379.title: Hilltop Settlements
j379.detail: Settlements for lookout and defense appeared on mountaintops and hills. They are taken to show the tension of the time of the Great Wa Disturbance.

j380.title: Makimuku Site Emerges
j380.detail: A large settlement forms at Makimuku in the Nara Basin. Its relation to the later Yamato court draws attention.

j381.title: Import of Iron
j381.detail: Iron material is carried from the southern Korean Peninsula, and chiefs in many regions competed over it.

j382.title: Hashihaka Tomb
j382.detail: The Hashihaka Tomb in Nara is among the oldest giant keyhole-shaped tombs. Some say it is Himiko's tomb, but this is not settled.

j383.title: Triangular-Rimmed Mirrors with Deities and Beasts
j383.detail: Many mirrors with a triangular-pointed rim are found in tombs in many regions. One theory says the Kinai court distributed them.

j384.title: Compilation of the Wei Zhi's Account of Wa
j384.detail: Part of the Records of the Three Kingdoms, it records the customs of Wa and the route to Yamatai. It remains a subject of debate.

j385.title: Seven-Branched Sword
j385.detail: A sword said to have been given from Baekje to Wa, kept at Isonokami Shrine. Its inscription conveys the diplomacy of the time.

j386.title: Horse Gear and Equestrian Culture
j386.detail: Horses and horse gear came from the continent and appeared among tomb grave goods. Both ways of fighting and ways of moving changed.

j387.title: Haniwa
j387.detail: Clay figures lined around tombs. Their forms of houses, people and horses tell us about life at the time.

j388.title: Arrival of Chinese Characters (Wani)
j388.detail: Wani of Baekje is said to have brought the Analects and the Thousand Character Classic. The dates in the tradition vary.

j389.title: Skills of the Migrants
j389.detail: Migrants such as the Hata and Aya clans passed on skills in silk-raising, weaving, civil engineering and ironmaking.

j390.title: Sue Ware Arrives
j390.detail: Hard pottery fired at high temperature with a potter's wheel and kiln came from the Korean Peninsula, and later became the origin of Japanese ceramics.

j391.title: Sword from Eta Funayama Tomb
j391.detail: A sword from a tomb in Kumamoto has an inscription suggestive of "Great King Wakatakeru." It is an important source alongside the Inariyama sword.

j392.title: Accession of Emperor Keitai
j392.detail: Prince Ohodo, said to be a fifth-generation descendant of Emperor Ojin, is welcomed by powerful clans and takes the throne.

j393.title: Doctors of the Five Classics from Baekje
j393.detail: Doctors versed in the Confucian classics come from Baekje, helping bring in learning and institutions.

j394.title: Soga no Iname Becomes Omi
j394.detail: The Soga clan became involved in the court's finances and the management of migrants, and expanded its power.

j395.title: Accession of Emperor Kinmei
j395.detail: Around Emperor Kinmei's time, conflict between the Soga and Mononobe deepened and led to the dispute over accepting Buddhism.

j396.title: End of Keyhole-Shaped Tombs
j396.detail: By the end of the 6th century, giant keyhole-shaped tombs were no longer built. The way of showing power shifts to temples.

j397.title: Shitenno-ji Founded
j397.detail: Prince Shotoku is said to have built Shitenno-ji in Osaka. Buddhism was accepted as a pillar of nation-building as well.

j398.title: Edict to Promote Buddhism
j398.detail: Empress Suiko orders respect for Buddhism, and the powerful clans compete to build temples.

j399.title: First Mission to Sui China
j399.detail: The Book of Sui records a visit by an envoy of Wa to the Sui. To shape itself as a state, Wa sought to learn from continental institutions.

j400.title: Calendar Arrives
j400.detail: The Baekje monk Kanroku brings books on the calendar, astronomy and divination. Knowledge for reading the seasons also bore on state politics.

j401.title: "Son of Heaven in the Land of the Rising Sun"
j401.detail: The letter Ono no Imoko carried contained wording showing equal standing with Sui, and is said to have angered the Sui emperor.

j402.title: Paper and Ink Arrive
j402.detail: The Goguryeo monk Damjing is said to have passed on how to make paper, ink and pigments.

j403.title: Founding of Tang
j403.detail: The Sui fall and the Tang is established. Tang institutions and culture would later greatly influence Japan through the envoys.

j404.title: Death of Prince Shotoku
j404.detail: The prince dies at Ikaruga Palace. Soga tyranny then grows stronger, and the prince's family is destroyed.

j405.title: Shaka Triad at Horyu-ji
j405.detail: A gilt-bronze Shaka triad made by Kuratsukuri no Tori. A representative work of Asuka sculpture, said to be for the repose of Prince Shotoku.

j406.title: Destruction of Prince Yamashiro no Oe
j406.detail: Soga no Iruka attacks the family of Prince Yamashiro no Oe, son of Prince Shotoku, and drives them to suicide.

j407.title: Isshi Incident
j407.detail: Prince Naka no Oe and others kill Soga no Iruka at Asuka Itabuki Palace, and Soga no Emishi also takes his own life. The opening of the Taika Reforms.

j408.title: Edict on Simple Burials
j408.detail: It curbs the enlargement of tombs and orders simpler funerals. Showing power through giant tombs came to an end.

j409.title: Naniwa Nagara no Toyosaki Palace
j409.detail: Emperor Kotoku builds a grand palace in Naniwa. It became the stage for the new institutions.

j410.title: Abe no Hirafu's Northern Expeditions
j410.detail: Moving north along the Sea of Japan coast, he negotiated and fought with the Emishi and Mishihase. A forerunner of the later management of Tohoku.

j411.title: Capital Moved to Omi Otsu Palace
j411.detail: After the defeat at Hakusukinoe, Emperor Tenji moves the capital to Omi with national defense in mind.

j412.title: Japan's First Water Clock
j412.detail: The Nihon Shoki says Emperor Tenji made a water clock (rokoku) and bells were struck to announce the time.

j413.title: Accession of Emperor Tenmu
j413.detail: Prince Oama, victor of the Jinshin War, takes the throne at Asuka Kiyomihara Palace. With strong authority he put the state's machinery in order.

j414.title: Silla Unifies the Peninsula
j414.detail: Silla drives out Tang forces and unifies the Korean Peninsula. Japan kept feeling out its relations with Silla and Tang.

j415.title: Yakusa no Kabane
j415.detail: The rank order of powerful clans is reorganized into eight kabane titles. A hierarchy with the emperor at the top took shape.

j416.title: Accession of Empress Jito
j416.detail: Carrying on her husband Tenmu's aims, she advances the building of the ritsuryo state. The Kōin household register was also made.

j417.title: Yakushi-ji Built
j417.detail: The temple Tenmu vowed for his ailing empress (Jito) is built in Fujiwara-kyo. It was later moved to Heijo-kyo.

j418.title: Murals of Takamatsuzuka Tomb
j418.detail: In the stone chamber of Takamatsuzuka Tomb in Nara, brightly colored groups of men and women and the Four Guardian Deities were painted. Discovered in 1972.

j419.title: Coin Hoarding Rank Law
j419.detail: A law granting rank to those who accumulated coins. It aimed to get currency circulating, but did not go well.

j420.title: Abe no Nakamaro Goes to Tang China
j420.detail: He crossed to Tang as a student with the missions and served Emperor Xuanzong. He could not return home and died in Tang.

j421.title: Compilation of the Yoro Code
j421.detail: Fujiwara no Fuhito and others revise the Taiho Code to make the Yoro Code. It was put into force in 757.

j422.title: Plan to Reclaim a Million Cho of Land
j422.detail: To increase farmland and stabilize tax revenue, land clearing was encouraged throughout the country.

j423.title: Accession of Emperor Shomu
j423.detail: An emperor deeply devoted to Buddhism. Large-scale projects followed, such as the founding of provincial temples and Todai-ji.

j424.title: Bohai Envoys Come to Japan
j424.detail: An embassy from the state of Bohai visits Japan for the first time. Exchange continued for 200 years.

j425.title: Hospital and Relief Houses
j425.detail: Empress Komyo is said to have set up the Segyakuin and Hiden'in for the sick and the poor.

j426.title: Kibi no Makibi Returns
j426.detail: The student Kibi no Makibi brought back to Japan books on Tang learning, music, military science and more.

j427.title: Successive Deaths of the Four Fujiwara Brothers
